title: Four moves, one real decision.
moves: What am I assuming, and which assumption needs testing?
How would this fail? Write the protest before a losing bidder does.
Give me ten options, including three we would never consider.
Play the person I am about to face. Then tell me what I missed.
foot: Approved tools. Fictional details. No invented facts or legal citations. People verify and decide.
notes: 2:49. Two minutes. The four moves map to what the program promised: a challenger (moves one and two), a brainstorming partner (move three), a sounding board (move four). Read the four moves out loud. That is the whole toolkit. Set the rhythm, same as this morning. I run it live on one example for about two, you run it on yours for three, one minute to compare with a neighbor. Have them pick their decision now, before the first move. A real one, nothing sensitive: a cooperative contract versus a fresh solicitation, whether to split a scope, how to handle a department that wants a bid waiver. Something they are actually chewing on. Thirty seconds, write it at the top of the page. That decision is the thread for the next twenty-four minutes. The example you will use on screen: a department has asked to piggyback on a cooperative contract for a software system rather than run a solicitation. Fictional enough to be safe, real enough that every buyer in the room has lived it. Transition: "Move one. The question I ask before every recommendation."
